articles.title: Karnataka CM Shivakumar writes to PM Modi seeking urgent intervention to resolve sugarcane farmers’ agitation
articles.description: Bengaluru, Oct 19 (IANS) Karnataka Chief Minister, D.K. Shivakumar, has written to Prime Minister Narendra Modi seeking urgent intervention to address the demands of sugarcane farmers, as protests in North Karnataka have delayed the commencement of the crushing season. In his three-page letter on Monday, CM Shivakumar urged the Centre to take early decisions on five key demands, including revision of the Minimum Selling Price (MSP) of sugar, separate prices for domestic and commercial sugar, changes in cane-based ethanol procurement and pricing, and restoration of the base recovery rate for fixing the Fair and Remunerative Price (FRP) at 9.50 per cent. Sugarcane farmers in North Karnataka have been protesting at various places and undertaking padayatras from different towns towards Hubballi, intending to gherao the residence of Union Minister Pralhad Joshi. Road blockades have also been reported at several locations. The Karnataka High Court has issued directions restraining the proposed protest at Joshi’s residence. Custom Ad: Multiplex CM Shivakumar said he visited Kittur in Belagavi district on October 17 and appealed to the protesting farmers to call off their padayatra. However, the farmers maintained that their principal demands fell within the Centre’s purview and that they would not withdraw the agitation without an assurance from the Union government. Describing the situation as grave, CM Shivakumar said the crushing season had not commenced in North Karnataka, leaving mature sugarcane standing in fields. Every day of delay was resulting in losses in cane weight and sugar content, he said. The continuing road blockades were also disrupting public order and causing considerable hardship to the general public. The Chief Minister said the state government had taken all measures available within its powers to address the concerns of farmers. Under a government order dated November 27, 2023, the Legal Metrology Department had issued a Standard Operating Procedure to prevent irregularities in sugar mill weighbridges, and all mills had been directed to comply. All 81 operational mills had shifted from analogue to digital load cells. District-level teams had also been constituted to inspect sugar recovery and cane weight at every mill at least twice a month during the 2025-26 season and submit reports to the state government. These measures had helped increase average sugar recovery from 9.91 per cent in 2022-23 to 11.09 per cent in 2025-26. All mills had also been directed to obtain accreditation from the National Accreditation Board for Testing and Calibration Laboratories (NABL) for their recovery-testing laboratories. CM Shivakumar said the state had ensured an additional Rs 100 per tonne over and above the price agreed upon by mills for the 2025-26 season through Government Order. The state government had borne Rs 50 per tonne of this additional amount from its own funds, and around Rs 290 crore had been paid directly to farmers. However, he said the farmers’ core demands could be addressed only by the Centre. Karnataka welcomed the committee constituted by the Union government on October 14 under the chairmanship of former NITI Aayog member Ramesh Chand to examine issues concerning sugarcane farmers and the sugar sector. The state would participate fully and share its data, CM Shivakumar said, adding that urgent decisions were necessary even as the committee continued its work. Among the key demands, CM Shivakumar sought revision of the sugar MSP, which has remained at Rs 31 per kg since February 14, 2019, despite the FRP increasing from Rs 2,750 to Rs 3,650 per tonne. He said mills could not pay farmers a fair price for sugarcane when the price of sugar remained at its 2019 level. He also sought separate MSPs for domestic and commercial sugar to protect household consumers while ensuring that bulk commercial buyers paid a fair price. The Chief Minister urged the Centre to review the exclusion of ethanol produced from sugarcane juice, sugar syrup and B-heavy molasses from the procurement tender issued by oil marketing companies on October 16 for the Ethanol Supply Year 2026-27, covering November 2026 to October 2027. Ethanol produced from C-heavy molasses remained eligible under the tender. Karnataka has a cane-based ethanol production capacity of 225 crore litres annually. Shivakumar said excluding these feedstocks could adversely affect sugar mills’ revenue and constrain their ability to make timely payments to farmers. He sought a review of the decision and a fair allocation for cane-based ethanol production in proportion to mills’ installed capacity. He further sought revision of ethanol prices for products made from sugarcane juice and B-heavy molasses, which had remained unchanged since 2022-23 despite annual increases in the FRP payable for sugarcane. In contrast, prices of grain-based ethanol had been revised upwards over the years. Another demand was the restoration of the FRP base recovery rate to 9.50 per cent from the current 10.25 per cent. Shivakumar said the base recovery rate had been increased in stages and that FRP was reduced when recovery fell below the prescribed level. He argued that sugar recovery depended on soil, climate and the timing of crushing, factors beyond farmers’ control. Consequently, farmers in low-recovery areas were unable to receive even the base FRP. CM Shivakumar urged PM Modi to intervene urgently, saying a clear and timely announcement on the demands would help the state government persuade farmers to withdraw their agitation and allow the crushing season to begin without further delay. He said an early decision was necessary in the interests of lakhs of sugarcane farmers and the people of Karnataka. --IANS mka/rad

articles.title: COVER STORY: India's Solar Opportunities & The Challenges Ahead
articles.description: 01 / THE BOTTLENECK What Are The Key Challenges In India’s Solar Market? Most seasoned industry leaders said that while India is making progressive strides towards adopting solar power, several bottlenecks continue to hinder its growth. Going forward, the biggest challenge will be to integrate growing solar into the grid, and to match it with demand profiles, which peaks during non-solar hours. This will require extensive planning, significant investment in expanding and modernizing grid infrastructure, and in supporting growth of energy storage to enable “peak shifting”. So, between now and 2030, we think the challenge is less about adding more gigawatts, and more about grid integration. Srivatsan Iyer, Global CEO, Hero Future Energies ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- As solar penetration rises, the challenge is that incremental generation is concentrated in the same daylight hours. The issue therefore shifts from the cost of producing a unit of solar electricity to its value to the grid at the time it is produced. We have already seen this globally through curtailment, low or even negative prices during high renewable hours and increasing evening flexibility requirements and these scenarios are emerging in India too. Deepak Thakur, MD & CEO, Hinduja Renewables India’s renewable-energy sector is entering a period of very strong growth and is among the most remarkable story globally. Demand is expanding rapidly, particularly from commercial and industrial customers and from new areas such as data centres and AI infrastructure. The opportunity for solar and hybrid renewable energy is therefore very significant. The next phase will be about managing that growth effectively – ensuring that generation, infrastructure, technology and storage evolve together with rising demand. Kuldeep Jain, Founder & MD, Cleanmax Module capacity has moved well ahead of cell capacity, and cells are well ahead of wafers and ingots, which are still largely imported. As ALMM List-II for cells comes into effect, with a limited transition window for certain projects, the real test is whether domestic cell capacity can keep pace with module demand. A sector that assembles at home but depends on others for its core components has not yet secured its energy sovereignty. Closing that gap, cells first and then wafers and ingots, is the biggest task between now and 2030. Sohan Lal Agarwal, CMD, Websol Energy System Limited In some regions, renewable capacity is growing faster than transmission and evacuation infrastructure, leading to grid congestion, curtailment and project delays. Ensuring that transmission and grid infrastructure keeps pace with generation will therefore be critical to fully utilising the renewable capacity India is adding. The biggest challenge will be moving from adding solar capacity to integrating it. Rupul Gupta, Founder, MD and CEO, TrueRE Orion Power Transmission delays, curtailment risks in resource-rich states and the gap between when the sun shines and when India actually needs power are the real constraints. Closely tied to this is the financial health of distribution companies. Developers can only scale with confidence if offtake is reliable and payments are timely. And we cannot ignore supply-chain dependence. Reducing reliance on imported cells, wafers and polysilicon is essential for long-term resilience. Harsan Patel, Whole Time Director, KPI Green Energy 02 / THE STORAGE QUESTION Solar and storage: how soon is the marriage inevitable? There is an agreement that storage will play an important role. Speakers highlighted that solar power and BESS are gradually becoming inseparable, with their integration expected to become more prominent. When we began building solar plants, the conversation was only about megawatts and tariffs. Today, every serious discussion we have with a DISCOM or a large customer comes back to one question: Can you give us power when we actually need it? Solar alone cannot answer that question. Solar with storage can. We see this in our own portfolio. Just a few years ago, storage was treated as an experiment. Today it is part of the project everyone asks about first. Venugopal Rao Maddireddy, CMD, Pace Digitek Ltd Rooftop solar and batteries are expected to converge in India over the next decade, shifting from an optional add-on to a standard configuration, led by commercial and industrial consumers. There are several reasons why the rooftop solar plus storage market is poised to grow. Time-of-day tariffs, which have been introduced for a larger number of consumers in several states, change more during peak hours of electricity use, such as the evening. Pawan Garg, CMD, Fujiyama As solar penetration rises, managing intermittency, transmission, land, curtailment and evening peak demand will become increasingly important. India’s electricity demand is also rising at night, particularly due to cooling, while solar generation falls after sunset. The sector therefore needs to focus not just on adding GW, but on evacuation infrastructure, storage, forecasting and system flexibility. Gautam Mohanka, Director, Gautam Solar Every new solar tender now carries a minimum two-hour storage requirement at 10% of capacity. SECI’s latest FDRE tender is 1,200 MW with 4,800 MWh BESS attached. Such bids will be standard practice now. That demand pulls storage, and storage pulls everything else. The next phase of solar growth will be decided by who is buying, not by what we are building. Without grid expansion and large-scale BESS, we are forcing assets to sit idle and bleed revenue. Sanjeev Agarwal, Founder and Chairman, Hexa Climate The market is shifting from simply buying low-cost renewable power to asking for firm, peak-hour and more reliable supply. That naturally increases the role of storage. For commercial and industrial users, adoption will depend on battery costs, tariff structures and the value of backup and peak-demand management. Residential adoption is likely to be more selective for some time, depending on local economics and reliability needs. Ishver Dholakia, Founder & MD, Goldi Solar The CEA has proposed that new ground-mounted solar and wind projects commissioned after July 2027 include co-located storage. Firm-power tenders already demand four hours of storage. The bigger change is in what the industry sells. The unit of value is moving from megawatts of capacity installed to megawatt-hours delivered on demand. Winners will be those who can design, integrate and guarantee dispatch, not just those who install panels at the lowest cost. Raju Komaravolu, CEO, Energy & Capital Goods (India), Zetwerk As solar penetration increases, four things will decide success: strengthening transmission and power evacuation, adding battery storage and forecasting for grid flexibility, speeding up land acquisition and connectivity approvals, and reducing financing costs and regulatory uncertainty. We also need deeper domestic manufacturing beyond module assembly for long-term energy security. Col Pravir Mishra, COO, Insolare Energy Limited With domestic cell requirements taking effect from June 2026, strengthening the upstream ecosystem is critical. Wafers and ingots still remain largely import-dependent, underlining the need to deepen domestic manufacturing across the value chain. The second challenge is transmission, taking operational capacity to approximately 8.5 GW, while solar-plus-four-hour-storage tariffs have fallen to ₹2.70–2.76 per kWh. Policy support through viability-gap funding is also helping accelerate adoption. Ankit Singhania, Director, Navitas Solar 03 / THE GROWTH DRIVER What are the next big drivers of solar growth? Industry leaders also shared their views on the potential drivers of growth in India’s solar market. These included agrivoltaics, floating solar, and other emerging solar applications. Beyond conventional utility-scale and rooftop solar, major growth drivers for India include solar-plus-storage, data-centre power demand in the commercial and industrial segment, and new applications such as floating solar and agrivoltaics. Green hydrogen also has significant long-term potential, particularly for industries such as steel, refining and fertilisers, but its growth will depend on achieving commercially viable production costs. Harendra Tomar, Leader – Business Development, Sungrow As solar penetration increases, the industry will also have to address land availability, project execution, financing and regulatory timelines more efficiently. These are not challenges for developers alone; they require coordination across the entire energy ecosystem. I believe the period to 2030 will mark a shift from capacity-led growth to system-led growth. The winners of the next phase will be those who can look beyond the solar plant itself and understand the complete journey of power—from generation to transmission, storage and consumption. Ravi Patel, Director – Sales & Marketing, Knack Energy India’s next phase of solar growth will be shaped by emerging technologies such as floating solar, agrivoltaics and green hydrogen, supported by battery energy storage systems (BESS) and grid modernisation. Generating more solar power is only part of the story. The larger task is making that power reliable, flexible and available when it is needed. We see agrivoltaics as a promising way to expand solar capacity. Simarpreet Singh, Executive Director and CEO, Hartek Power One of the key constraints today is the availability of suitable land and adequate evacuation infrastructure for large-scale projects. In this context, alternative models such as floating solar and agrivoltaics are poised to gain traction in the near term. Among these, agrivoltaics holds particular promise, as it enables dual use of land—supporting both agriculture and energy generation. With the right policy incentives and regulatory support, agrivoltaics could emerge as a highly efficient and scalable solution for India’s next phase of solar growth. Tanmoy Duari, , Acix Energy India Pvt. Limited India has 140M farmers. Agrivoltaics (solar + farming on same land) solves land conflict. PM KUSUM already is targeting 34 GW. With elevated structures, farmer earns Rs 40k/acre from solar + crop income. This is bankable because farmer gets dual income, and you get land without acquisition headache. Gujarat & Maharashtra are already financing at scale. India has 18,000 sq km of reservoirs. No land cost, 10% higher yield due to cooling are added benefits. Vikass Agarwwal, Founder & CEO, DebtBridge We see the next growth coming from solar that fits into everyday life and from new applications creating demand for clean electricity. Distributed solar added about 16.3 GW in FY26, over a third of the year's additions. Floating solar is a good example of thinking ahead. India has only about 700 MW today, against a NISE potential of around 102 GW. The new PM Surya Sarovar Yojana backs 5,000 MW with 10,000 MWh of storage, and it uses water bodies instead of competing for land. Rajesh Kaushal, EIS Business Group Head (India & SAARC), Delta Electronics India So far, lower power cost was the driver but from here on, decarbonization, green economy and net zero will be the bigger drivers of Solar energy growth in next decade. The government has mandated that minimum 10% of the storage is required so definitely storage and Solar will go together. Eventually if we consider NET ZERO targets we need to store maximum solar energy into the battery and use them during non-solar hour. Bharat Chhittarkka, Managing Director, Trex Energy The one thing people underestimate is commercial and industrial demand. Green open access rules have been eased, and companies now have R100 targets and export customers to answer to, especially with CBAM in force in Europe. Clean power is becoming a procurement requirement for Indian industry, not a CSR line. On the residential side, PM Surya Ghar has taken rooftop solar into tier-2 and tier-3 towns. Together, distributed solar is turning into a large market in its own right. Deepak Jain, CTO, INA Solar Green hydrogen, floating solar and agrivoltaics each have strong potential. Green hydrogen can help industries cut emissions. Floating solar makes use of water bodies, and agrivoltaics allows farming and power generation on the same land. What they share is that they all extend solar beyond the traditional rooftop and ground-mounted plant. We believe the next phase of growth will come from solar combined with storage and tailored to specific needs, such as industrial power, land-constrained areas and farming communities. How fast each one grows will depend on falling costs, supportive policy and successful pilot projects. Sunsure Energy 04 / A SNEAK PEEK INTO THE FUTURE Where is the solar market heading to? Several industry leaders also offered a glimpse into the future of India’s solar market, drawing on past learnings, evolving policies, emerging trends, and other key developments shaping the sector. More tenders now require solar with storage, round-the-clock supply or firm power. What we’re still waiting for is the economics and the market rules to catch up so this can accelerate. The government is helping. Phase III of the Green Energy Corridor has just been approved, at Rs 1.86 lakh crore, and it should help move up to 135 GW of renewable power and add 50 GWh of battery storage. Standalone solar will continue to make economic sense where daytime demand exists or the grid can absorb the generation. But as more solar enters the same daytime window, simply adding generation does not solve the larger power system requirement. The next unit of renewable capacity increasingly must solve for when power is required, not merely how much can be generated. In my view, storage becomes inseparable from utility-scale solar by regulation around 2027–28, and from C&I solar by economics in the states that move first. The bigger change is in what the industry sells. The unit of value is moving from megawatts of capacity installed to megawatt-hours delivered on demand. Winners will be those who can design, integrate and guarantee dispatch, not just those who install panels at the lowest cost. By 2030, I do not expect storage to be standard across every solar project. However, I do expect it to become a much more important part of how solar is planned and valued, especially since a significant amount of energy generated today is going unused or being wasted. The conversation will gradually shift from how cheaply solar can generate power to when that power can be delivered and how reliably it can meet demand. Ishver Dholakia, MD, Goldi Solar The economics have also turned decisively. When Madhya Pradesh can secure solar-plus-storage power at a record-low Rs 2.70 per unit, the argument that storage is too expensive is simply over. Regulators have noticed too. Maharashtra now requires battery storage with new rooftop solar above 100 kW, and we expect other states to follow sooner than people think. Beyond generation, the convergence of solar with green hydrogen, green ammonia, data centres and other energy-intensive applications is creating entirely new consumption models. This broader convergence is reflected in our SCALE strategy, where we are leveraging technology, AI and partnerships and expanding into emerging clean-energy applications and new forms of energy consumption. Rupul Gupta, Founder, MD & CEO, TrueRE Orion Power Buyers want reliable, round-the-clock supply, and the best answer will vary by region, resource and load profile. Wind-solar hybrid, and batteries will each have a role, and many projects will combine them. We serve round-the-clock needs today through wind-solar hybrid solutions, which complement storage. We expect this integrated approach to become the norm for new large-scale and commercial and industrial projects over the next four to five years. Kuldeep Jain, Founder and MD, CleanMax But the real driver is on the demand side, not the supply side. Data centres. Companies like Google, Microsoft and Amazon are buying firm clean power at a scale that changes what we build, and they will not sign a contract that looks green on paper while drawing coal after sunset. That demand pulls storage, and storage pulls everything else. The next phase of solar growth will be decided by who is buying, not by what we are building.

articles.title: Poor contractor response delays Telangana STP tenders under HAM
articles.description: Telangana has extended STP tender deadlines to November 2 after contractors raised concerns over payments under the Hybrid Annuity Model. The Rs 1,314-crore project covers 101 urban local bodies across three packages, with Central and State funding arrangements proposed.

articles.title: India bars sugar-based ethanol from 2026-27 tender, cuts maize ethanol price
articles.description: New Delhi: State-run oil marketing companies (OMCs) have excluded ethanol produced from sugarcane juice, sugar syrup and B-heavy molasses from their latest procurement tender for the 2026-27 supply year, as the government seeks to safeguard domestic sugar supplies while maintaining its nationwide ethanol-blended petrol programme, PTI reported. The tender, issued by Bharat Petroleum Corporation Limited […] The post India bars sugar-based ethanol from 2026-27 tender, cuts maize ethanol price appeared first on BioEnergy Times.
